title: Private Deployments — VPC & On‑Prem Reference Architectures, Packaging, Day‑2 Ops, and Upgrade/Rollback
author: Samantha Chen
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s canonical guidance for private deployments (VPC and on‑prem). It includes: reference architectures, on‑prem packaging checklist, day‑2 operational procedures, upgrade and rollback playbooks, and the customer requirements library to use for scoping/proposals. Intended audience: platform engineers, SREs, solutions engineers, and security reviewers.

Purpose and scope:
- Provide a single, implementation‑level reference that productionizes private deployments while meeting security, compliance, and reliability SLOs.
- Covers two deployment flavors: VPC-hosted private control plane with customer network peering (recommended for most customers), and fully on‑prem (air‑gapped) packaging for regulated/air‑gapped environments.
- Assumes familiarity with Kubernetes, helm/tgz packaging, and basic networking (BGP, VPN, VPC peering).

Owners and contacts:
- Primary owner: Private Deployments team (eng-private-deployments).
- Oncall contact: eng-private-deployments@redwood.internal (pager: #private-deployments-oncall).
- Security reviewer: Aisha Patel (security).

Goals and SLOs:
- Control plane API latency: 95th percentile < 250ms for control API calls within same region.
- Serving availability (customer‑facing inference endpoints): 99.95% monthly for Dedicated/Private clusters under normal load.
- Upgrade success rate: >= 98% automated upgrade success across staged rollouts.
- Recovery RTO for node replacement: < 15 minutes for a single worker GPU node.

1) Reference architectures (summary)
A. VPC-hosted private deployment (recommended)
- Components: private control plane (hosted by Redwood in customer VPC peered account), customer-managed serving clusters (EKS/GKE/AKS or on‑prem k8s), secure ingress (NLB/ALB with mTLS), centralized observability (Grafana/Tempo/Prometheus federated), KMS integration (customer KMS), and private artifact registry.
- Typical network flows:
  1. Control plane <-> Serving control plane agents: TLS over private peering or AWS Transit Gateway.
  2. Serving node <-> Model storage: signed, short-lived URLs to S3 (or S3-compatible object store) within customer VPC.
  3. Telemetry: metrics and traces forwarded over an encrypted channel to a metrics endpoint in the customer VPC or to Redwood-managed endpoints per contract.
- Failure domains and HA: control plane pair across AZs, serving pool autoscaled with at least N+2 GPU capacity for critical workloads.

B. On‑prem (air‑gapped) deployment
- Components: offline package (tarball/OCI), local registry, curated kernel binaries for supported GPU families, bundle of container images, package install script, and an optional local control plane (if customer requires full air gap).
- Constraints: no external egress except to internal registries; time synchronization required (NTP), hardware compatibility matrix enforced.

Reference architecture diagrams (textual)
- VPC: [Control Plane in Partner Account] <-> [Customer VPC (Transit Gateway / Peering)] -> [Serving Cluster (EKS) w/ GPU nodes] -> [Object Store / KMS]
- On‑prem: [Admin Workstation] -> [Local Registry / Artifact Server] -> [K8s Cluster w/ GPU Nodes] -> [Local Object Store / KMS Appliance]

2) Pre-deployment customer requirements library (checklist to validate before engagement)
- Account and network:
  - VPC ID(s), CIDR ranges, peering/transit gateway details, permitted ports (see network table below), and cross-account role ARNs for control-plane access.
  - Public IPs: reserved set for NAT/egress (if required).
- Security and compliance:
  - KMS type: AWS KMS / CloudHSM / customer HSM details and key rotation policy.
  - Compliance constraints: SOC2, HIPAA, PCI — identify documents to exchange and scope of allowed telemetry.
- Hardware and OS:
  - GPU SKU and driver versions (supported: NVIDIA A10/A100/H100, driver >=450.x for A100; check packaging matrix).
  - Kubernetes distribution and versions (supported: EKS 1.26+, GKE 1.26+, upstream k8s 1.25+).
  - Disk and throughput requirements: local NVMe for model cache (recommended >= 1TB for models > 20B), bandwidth to object store >= 2 Gbps for initial model pulls.
- IAM and RBAC:
  - Service account ARNs or cross-account role for control-plane agent.
  - RBAC policy attachments for namespace-level operators (list provided in appendix).
- Observability:
  - Metrics endpoint (Prometheus scraping target or push gateway), log aggregation endpoint (Fluentd/Fluent Bit), and tracing collector endpoint.
- Backup and disaster recovery:
  - Snapshot cadence for model store metadata and configuration (recommended daily), retention policy, and restore window expectations.

Network table (minimum ports):
- Control plane -> agent: TCP 443 (mTLS), keepalive 30s
- Agent -> object store: TCP 443 (HTTPS)
- Serving nodes -> model cache: TCP 2049 (if using NFS) or S3-compatible endpoints
- Metrics scraping: TCP 9090 (Prometheus) or push gateway endpoints

3) Packaging and installation (on‑prem / air‑gapped)
A. Packaging artifacts
- bundle.tgz: includes Helm charts, container images (OCI layout) or image tarballs, curated kernel libs, driver compatibility matrix, and install scripts.
- checksums.txt and signed_manifest.json (GPG-signed manifest for binary verification).

B. Suggested install flow (air‑gapped)
1. Preflight on admin workstation: verify SHA256 of bundle, confirm hardware and kernel versions.
2. Load images into local registry: registryctl load --tar bundle/images.tar
3. Helm install of platform components in order: storage -> cert-manager -> control-agent -> runtime-operator -> serving-runtime -> observability
4. Post-install verification: smoke tests (see /tests/smoke/ directory in package)

C. Example Helm values snippet (k8s values.yaml excerpt):
```yaml
controlPlane: 
  enabled: false # when fully air-gapped we run control agents only
servingRuntime:
  replicas: 3
  resourceRequests:
    gpu: 1
  modelCache:
    sizeGi: 1024
observability:
  prometheus:
    enabled: true
    scrapeInterval: 30s
```

4) Day‑2 operations (runbook and run cadence)
A. Common day‑2 tasks
- Scaling: use the runtime autoscaler to add GPU nodes. Command: rwdctl cluster scale --pool=gpupool --count=+2
- Model rollout: publish model version metadata to model registry, instruct serving operator to prefetch on new nodes via PrefetchJob CRD.
- Cache invalidation: rwdctl cache invalidate --model-id <id> --prefix-length 256
- Certificate rotation: follow cert-rotation playbook (rotate certs every 90 days).

B. Routine checks (daily/weekly)
- Daily: check control-plane heartbeat, agent connectivity (>99% agents healthy), model pull error rate < 0.5%
- Weekly: verify SLOs, review top 5 latency outliers, disk utilization per node < 80%
- Monthly: run disaster recovery restore test in staging, validate KMS access rotation

C. Incident triage checklist (serving outage)
1. Confirm scope: Is issue control-plane-only or serving? Gather request IDs and trace IDs (ask app team for example trace).
2. Check control plane pods: kubectl -n rwd get pods; check restart counts and OOMs.
3. Check agent connectivity: rwdctl agents list --status=unhealthy.
4. If model pull failures: verify object store endpoint, signed URL expiry, and node disk pressure.
5. If GPU node failure: cordon + drain, then replace with new node; use node-replace playbook.
6. Engage SRE and file a postmortem for P1s per incident-process.

5) Upgrade and rollback procedures
A. Upgrade principles
- All upgrades must follow staged rollouts: canary (1–2 clusters/nodes) -> partial (10–30%) -> full.
- Maintain backward-compatible API contracts for control agents during upgrade window.
- Automated preflight must pass on canary before continuing. Abort on critical errors.

B. Upgrade checklist
- Pre-upgrade: snapshot configuration, export current model registry index, ensure at least 2x required spare capacity in serving pools.
- Run automated preflight (rwdctl upgrade preflight --target-version vX.Y.Z). Preconditions include: node drivers, kube version, free disk >= 20% per node, and successful e2e smoke tests.
- Canary upgrade: deploy to a single pool, monitor APDEX and error rate for 30–60 minutes.
- Roll forward: if canary stable, proceed to partial then full.
- Post-upgrade verification: run acceptance tests, validate latency distributions and token cost variance < 5% vs baseline.

C. Rollback procedure (immediate rollback option)
- Trigger: critical regression in production (latency SLO breach > 5% p95 increase or error rate spike > 1%).
- Steps:
  1. Pause rollout: rwdctl upgrade pause --deployment <id>
  2. Rollback agents: rwdctl upgrade rollback --to-version <previous-version> --scope <canary|partial|full>
  3. In case of data schema changes, run data-migration-rollback scripts in order specified in upgrade manifest.
  4. Restore configuration snapshot (if applicable) and validate service health.
  5. Open incident, notify stakeholders, and run RCA.

6) Monitoring, observability, and alerts
- Required dashboards: per-cluster latency, token cost per inference, KV cache hit ratio, GPU utilization, model pull error rate.
- Required alerts (examples):
  - Control-plane heartbeat missing for > 2 minutes -> P1 oncall notify.
  - Model pull failure rate > 1% over 5m -> P2.
  - GPU node OOM / driver crash -> P1.
  - Disk utilization > 90% -> P2.

7) Security & compliance considerations
- Network: enforce least-privilege security groups, deny all inbound by default and allow only required ports.
- Secrets: require KMS-wrapped secrets; do not store plaintext model tokens in config maps.
- Audit logging: enable object-store access logs and control-plane admin actions; retain per-contract (default 90 days).
- Vulnerability scanning: scan images before bundle creation; fail build on critical CVEs.

8) Appendices
A. Sample RBAC policy (short):
- API group: apps, resources: deployments, verbs: [get,list,watch,update] for namespace rwd-serving

B. Supported hardware matrix (summary):
- NVIDIA A10 (driver 470+), A100 (driver 450+), H100 (driver 535+) — check packaging manifest for exact kernel modules.

C. Example post-install smoke test commands:
- rwdctl healthcheck --component serving-runtime
- kubectl -n rwd logs -l app=serving-runtime --tail=100 | grep "startup complete"

D. Useful commands and scripts:
- rwdctl agents list --region us-west-2 --status=unhealthy
- rwdctl cluster scale --pool gpupool --count +2
- rwdctl upgrade preflight --target-version vX.Y.Z

Document maintenance and updates:
- This page is reviewed quarterly by the Private Deployments team and after every major release or significant incident. For changes to packaging or supported SKUs, update the packaging manifest and test matrix in the package repo.
